title: After five months of easy living, Pinocchio is amazed to find a fine pair of donkey ears growing, and becomes a little donkey, tail and all.
paragraphs: At last the wagon arrived: and it arrived without the slightest noise, because its wheels were wrapped in loose plant fibres and rags.
It was pulled by twelve pairs of little donkeys, all the same size, but with different coats.
Some were grey, others white, others speckled like salt and pepper, and others marked with broad yellow and blue stripes.

But the strangest thing was this: those twelve pairs, or twenty-four little donkeys, instead of wearing horseshoes like all the other animals that pulled or carried loads, wore little men's boots made of white leather.
And the driver of the wagon?…

Picture a little man wider than he was tall, soft and oily as a ball of butter, with a little rosy-apple face, a tiny mouth that was always smiling and a soft, sweet voice like a cat appealing to the kind heart of the lady of the house.

As soon as children saw him, they were all delighted with him and raced each other to climb onto his wagon, so he could take them to that true paradise known on the map by the tempting name of the Land of Toys.

Indeed, the wagon was already packed with boys between eight and twelve years old, piled on top of one another like anchovies in salty water. They were uncomfortable, they were squashed, they could hardly breathe: but nobody said “ow!” and nobody complained. The happy thought that in a few hours they would reach a country with no books, schools or teachers made them so pleased and willing to put up with things that they felt neither discomfort nor jolts, hunger, thirst or sleepiness.
As soon as the wagon stopped, the little man turned to Candlewick and, with a thousand little faces and gestures, asked him with a smile:
“Tell me, my handsome boy, would you like to come to that happy country too?”
“Of course I would!”
“But I must warn you, my dear, there's no room left in the wagon. As you can see, it's full!…”
“Never mind!” Candlewick replied. “If there's no room inside, I'll manage sitting on the wagon shafts.” And with a leap, he sat astride the long poles at the front.
“And you, my love,” said the little man, turning to Pinocchio with great politeness, “what do you intend to do? Are you coming with us or staying?…”
“I'm staying,” answered Pinocchio. “I want to go home: I want to study and do well at school, like all good boys.”
“Good luck to you!”
“Pinocchio,” said Candlewick then, “listen to me: come with us and we'll have fun!”
“No, no, no!”
“Come with us and we'll have fun!” shouted four more voices from inside the wagon.
“Come with us and we'll have fun!” a hundred voices yelled together.
“And if I come with you, what will my kind Fairy say?” asked the puppet, who was beginning to soften and change his mind.
“Don't fill your head with so many worries. Remember, we're going to a country where we'll be free to make a racket from morning till night!”
Pinocchio didn't answer, but gave a sigh; then he gave another sigh: then a third sigh: at last he said:
“Make a little room for me: I want to come too!…”
“All the places are taken,” replied the little man, “but to show you how welcome you are, I can give you my seat on the driver's box.”
“And what about you?”
“I'll walk.”
“Certainly not, I won't allow it. I'd rather climb onto the back of one of these little donkeys!” cried Pinocchio.

No sooner said than done, he went up to the right-hand donkey in the first pair and made to climb onto its back: but the little animal turned sharply, gave him a great butt in the stomach and knocked him head over heels.
Just imagine the rude, wild burst of laughter from all the boys watching.
But the little man did not laugh. He went up to the stubborn little donkey very lovingly and, pretending to kiss it, bit off half its right ear.

Meanwhile Pinocchio, getting up from the ground in a fury, sprang onto the poor animal's back. And it was such a splendid leap that the boys stopped laughing and began to shout, “Hooray for Pinocchio!” and clap their hands without stopping.
Then suddenly the little donkey raised both its back legs and gave such a mighty buck that it flung the poor puppet into the middle of the road, onto a heap of gravel.

There was another great burst of laughter: but instead of laughing, the little man felt so much love for the restless donkey that, with a kiss, he took off half its other ear. Then he said to the puppet:
“Climb back on, and don't be afraid. That little donkey had some silly ideas in its head: but I've whispered a word or two in its ears, and I hope I've made it gentle and sensible.”

Pinocchio climbed on, and the wagon began to move: but as the donkeys galloped and the wagon raced over the stones of the main road, the puppet thought he heard a low voice, so faint he could barely make it out, saying:
“Poor fool! You insisted on having your own way, but you'll regret it!”

Almost frightened, Pinocchio looked around to see where these words came from; but he saw no one: the donkeys galloped, the wagon raced along, the boys inside it slept, Candlewick snored like a dormouse, and the little man on the driver's box hummed under his breath:
“Everyone sleeps at night, But I never sleep…”
After another half-kilometre, Pinocchio heard the faint little voice say:

“Remember this, little fool! Boys who stop studying and turn their backs on books, schools and teachers, to spend all their time playing and having fun, can only come to a bad end! I know from experience, and I can tell you!… One day you'll cry too, as I'm crying today… but then it will be too late!…”
At these softly whispered words, the puppet, more frightened than ever, jumped down from his mount and went to hold his little donkey by the muzzle.
And imagine how he felt when he discovered that his little donkey was crying… and crying just like a boy!
“Hey, little gentleman,” Pinocchio shouted to the owner of the wagon, “do you know what's happening? This little donkey is crying.”
“Let him cry: he'll laugh on his wedding day!”
“But have you taught him to talk as well?”
“No: he learned to mumble a few words by himself, after spending three years with a group of trained dogs.”
“Poor animal!…”
“Come, come…” said the little man, “let's not waste our time watching a donkey cry. Climb back on, and let's go: the night is cool, and the road is long.”
Pinocchio obeyed without a word. The wagon set off again: and at dawn they arrived safely in the Land of Toys.

This country was like no other country in the world. Its people were all boys. The oldest were fourteen: the youngest were barely eight. In the streets there was enough joy, noise and shouting to drive you out of your mind! Gangs of boys everywhere: some played with nuts, some with throwing tiles, some with balls, some rode bicycles, some rode little wooden horses: these played blind man's buff; those chased each other: others, dressed as clowns, swallowed burning plant fibres: some acted, some sang, some did somersaults, some amused themselves walking on their hands with their legs in the air: some rolled hoops, some marched around dressed as generals with paper helmets and papier-mâché swords: some laughed, some yelled, some called, some clapped, some whistled, some copied the sound of a hen that has laid an egg: in short, there was such chaos, such chatter, such a wild racket that you had to put cotton wool in your ears to keep from being deafened. In every square stood little canvas theatres, packed with boys from morning till night, and on all the walls you could read lovely things written in charcoal, like these: “Hooray for toyz!” instead of “toys”; “We dont wont skools” instead of “We don't want schools”; “Down with arithmatick” instead of “arithmetic”, and other fine examples like them.

As soon as Pinocchio, Candlewick and all the other boys who had travelled with the little man set foot in the town, they plunged straight into the great uproar, and within minutes, as you can easily imagine, they were everyone's friends. Who could be happier, who could be more pleased than they were? With endless games and all kinds of fun, the hours, days and weeks passed like flashes of lightning.
“Oh, what a wonderful life!” Pinocchio said whenever he happened to run into Candlewick.

“So you see I was right?” the other replied. “And to think you didn't want to come! To think you'd got it into your head to go home to your Fairy and waste your time studying! If you're free today from the boredom of books and school, you owe it to me, my advice and my care for you, don't you agree? Only true friends know how to do such great favours.”

“It's true, Candlewick! If I'm a really happy boy today, it's all thanks to you. And do you know what the teacher used to say about you? He was always telling me: ‘Don't spend time with that rascal Candlewick, because Candlewick is a bad friend, and he can only advise you to do wrong!…’”
“Poor teacher!” the other replied, shaking his head. “I know only too well that he couldn't stand me and always enjoyed telling lies about me; but I'm generous, and I forgive him!”
“What a noble heart!” said Pinocchio, hugging his friend lovingly and kissing him between the eyes.

By now this wonderful life of playing and having fun all day, without ever seeing a book or a school, had lasted five months; when one morning Pinocchio woke up and got, as people say, a very nasty surprise, which put him in a thoroughly bad mood.
